title: Hardwired and microprogrammed control
subtitle: The control unit turns an opcode into the exact sequence of signals that move data through the machine.

micro.title: Micro-operations
micro.body: An instruction is carried out as a sequence of micro-operations, each a register-transfer that fits in one clock. Fetch, for example, is: MAR ← PC; MDR ← Memory[MAR]; IR ← MDR; PC ← PC + 1. A control word is the set of signals (which register loads, which bus is driven, what the ALU does) asserted in one step.

hard.title: Hardwired control
hard.body: A hardwired control unit generates signals with combinational logic: a step counter decoded to timing signals T1, T2…, an opcode decoder, and gates that AND them together (e.g. “load IR = T3”). It is very fast, but changing the instruction set means redesigning the logic — the usual choice for RISC.

mp.title: Microprogrammed control
mp.body: In a microprogrammed unit the control words are stored in a fast control memory. Each instruction’s opcode selects the start of a microroutine; a micro-program counter steps through it, reading one microinstruction per clock and sending its bits to the data path. A microinstruction also says what comes next: fall through, jump, or branch on a condition flag. Changing or extending the instruction set is just rewriting the microcode (Wilkes’ original idea), which is why CISC machines use it.
mp.steps: A machine has 64 micro-routines of at most 16 microinstructions each and 40 control signals. Control memory holds 64 × 16 = 1024 words. Each word carries the 40 signals plus a next-address field of ⌈log₂1024⌉ = 10 bits.

horiz.title: Horizontal and vertical microcode
horiz.body: Horizontal microinstructions give every control signal its own bit: wide, fast, highly parallel. Vertical ones encode the signals in fields (like opcodes) and need decoders: narrow but slower. Real designs mix them.

seq.title: Sequencing the microprogram
seq.body: After each microinstruction the next address comes from: the incremented µPC (most steps), a jump field, a conditional branch on a flag, a mapping from the opcode (at the start), or a stack for microsubroutines. Address generation is the control unit’s own program counter logic.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• Instructions = sequences of micro-operations; a control word drives one step.
  • Hardwired: fast, rigid. Microprogrammed: flexible, a bit slower.
  • Horizontal = wide and parallel; vertical = narrow and encoded.
